Gary: That sounds good, Ethan. I really could use some help organizing my schedule to make time for myself too.

Perspective: Ethan Mohamud.

I know Gary as my long-time friend from middle school. I’ve seen him overworking, skipping meals, and sacrificing sleep, so I invited him to a retreat because I was concerned. At the retreat, I noticed he was restless and avoided talking about work, which made me suspect there was more going on. When I confronted him, he opened up about the pressures of managing a new department and personal challenges.

In Scenario 3, now that I understand his circumstances, my intention is to help him practically: I suggest prioritizing tasks and delegating responsibilities so he can find better balance. I’m trying to help him solve the immediate problem.

In Scenario 4, after months of checking in, I can see Gary is actually making efforts to change. He tells me things are better, he’s less overwhelmed, and he even had time for a movie. From my perspective, he is no longer just revealing a problem—he is acting on it and showing early progress. That makes me feel hopeful and proud, so my intention shifts from directly helping him organize his schedule to encouraging him, checking in, and supporting his continued progress.

So the change in my intention is driven by what I observe after the confrontation: Gary’s efforts to change and his reported improvement. I am not yet stepping back as if he is fully independent—that comes later, in Scenario 5. The closest fit from my perspective is observing Gary’s efforts post-confrontation, with early signs of improvement.

- Expectation: A retreat might interrupt Gary’s routine, help him relax, and give him a new perspective, though he may resist.

Event-by-Event Analysis:

Event 1 — Scenario 1:
- Intention: Persuade Gary to accept help and go on the retreat; remains committed to helping even after Gary initially declines.
- Belief: Gary’s refusal confirms how strongly work is consuming him; he may not see the cost to his health.
- Emotion: Concern intensifies; disappointment and empathy at Gary’s refusal.
- Expectation: Gary may still be reachable if given the right opportunity; the retreat could reveal how strained he is.

Event 2 — Scenario 2:
- Intention: Gently confront Gary and get him to open up about what is really going on.
- Belief: Gary’s overwork is not just professional obligation; he is restless and avoiding work talk, so something deeper is being hidden.
- Emotion: Suspicion mixed with worry and empathy; concern about Gary’s burden.
- Expectation: A nonjudgmental approach may help Gary feel safe enough to disclose his problems.

Event 3 — Scenario 3:
- Intention: Provide practical, direct help—help Gary prioritize tasks, delegate responsibilities, and find better balance.
- Belief: Now that Gary has explained the new department pressures and personal challenges, the cause is clearer and partly manageable.
- Emotion: Relief at Gary’s disclosure, combined with empathy and continued concern.
- Expectation: Concrete planning and delegation can reduce Gary’s overload and create time for himself.

Event 4 — Scenario 4:
- Intention: Shift from directly fixing Gary’s schedule to checking in, encouraging, and supporting his continued progress.
- Belief: Gary is making genuine efforts and showing real improvement; he has agency and is becoming more capable of managing.
- Emotion: Hopeful, proud, supportive.
- Expectation: Gary can continue improving if encouraged; setbacks may happen, but progress is real.

Why the intention changes from Scenario 3 to Scenario 4:
In Scenario 3, Ethan’s intention is problem-solving because Gary has just revealed the hidden causes of his overwork. Ethan responds practically: organize tasks, delegate, find balance. In Scenario 4, after months of checking in, Ethan observes that Gary is actually acting on the advice and reporting improvement. Because Ethan’s belief changes from “Gary needs direct help” to “Gary is actively improving and capable,” his intention shifts from fixing the problem to encouraging and reinforcing progress. His emotion also shifts from relief/empathy to hope/pride, and his expectation shifts from possible improvement to likely sustained improvement.

Event 5 — Scenario 5:
- Intention: Step back and let Gary manage independently, while remaining available if needed.
- Belief: Gary has successfully adjusted to a healthier work-life balance and can maintain it on his own.
- Emotion: Satisfaction, happiness, pride, and calm affection.
- Expectation: Gary will sustain his progress; Ethan’s support becomes a standby safety net rather than active management.

Current Mental State:
- Intention: Be a supportive friend at a distance; step back, but remain available if Gary ever needs him.
- Belief: Gary is capable, has improved, and can manage his own work-life balance.
- Emotion: Satisfied, happy, proud, and affectionate toward Gary.
- Expectation: Gary will maintain his healthier balance, and their long friendship will remain a reliable source of support.
